entries.meaning: A place where planes take off and land, with buildings for passengers. ---
examples: Our flight leaves from the smaller airport across town.
Both airports were shut down by the storm.
We got to the airport three hours early.

entries.meaning: A company that carries passengers by plane. ---
examples: The airline lost my bag somewhere in Denver.
Several airlines fly that route nonstop.
I called the airline to change my seat.

entries.meaning: A vehicle with wings and engines that flies through the air. ---
examples: She has never been on an airplane before.
Small airplanes land at the county field.
The airplane was still sitting at the gate.
entries.contrast: Americans write airplane; the British write aeroplane.

entries.meaning: An airplane, in everyday speech. ---
examples: Our plane was delayed two hours in Chicago.
I hate taking small planes in bad weather.
We ran to catch the last plane out.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like plain (simple, ordinary).

entries.meaning: A building at an airport or station where passengers arrive and leave. ---
examples: International flights leave from terminal B.
The two terminals are connected by a train.
There's a coffee place at the far end of the terminal.

entries.meaning: The long strip of pavement where planes take off and land. ---
examples: We sat on the runway for forty minutes.
Ice closed both runways that morning.
The plane turned onto the runway and picked up speed.

entries.meaning: The front section of a plane where the pilots sit. ---
examples: The cockpit door stays locked during the flight.
Modern cockpits have almost no paper charts left.
A voice from the cockpit announced our altitude.

entries.meaning: The moment when a plane leaves the ground. ---
examples: Please keep your seat upright for takeoff.
Bad weather delayed takeoffs all afternoon.
My ears always pop right after takeoff.

entries.meaning: Rough air that shakes a plane during flight. ---
examples: We hit some turbulence over the mountains.
The turbulence lasted about ten minutes.
She's a nervous flyer, so any turbulence upsets her.

entries.meaning: A short stay in a city on the way to your final destination. ---
examples: We booked a two-day stopover in Reykjavik.
Free stopovers are part of the fare.
The stopover let us see the city for a day.

entries.meaning: The act of leaving on a plane, train, or bus. ---
examples: Our departure was pushed back an hour.
Departures are on the upper level.
Check the board for the departure time.

entries.meaning: The act of reaching a place at the end of a trip. ---
examples: Our arrival time is listed as 6:40.
Meet me downstairs in arrivals.
Rain greeted us on arrival.

entries.meaning: A second flight or train you change to in order to finish a trip. ---
examples: I almost missed my connection in Dallas.
There are only two connections a day to that island.
The gate agent rebooked my connection.

entries.meaning: The moving belt at an airport where checked bags come out. ---
examples: Our bags are on carousel four.
All the carousels were jammed with luggage.
I waited at the carousel for twenty minutes.

entries.meaning: A strap that holds you in your seat on a plane or in a car. ---
examples: Please fasten your seatbelt.
The seatbelts in the back row were twisted.
He never drives without his seatbelt on.

entries.meaning: The document that lets you get on a plane. ---
examples: Have your boarding pass ready at the gate.
Our boarding passes are saved on my phone.
I printed the boarding pass at the kiosk.

entries.meaning: A room that is free for someone to rent. ---
examples: The motel sign said no vacancy.
Call around; some place will have vacancies tonight.
We took the last vacancy in town.

entries.meaning: A comfortable waiting room at an airport or hotel. ---
examples: We waited in the airport lounge until boarding.
The hotel has two lounges off the lobby.
Her credit card gets her into the lounge for free.

entries.meaning: The tired, confused feeling you get after flying across time zones. ---
examples: I had terrible jet lag for three days.
Jet lag is worse flying east.
Coffee doesn't really fix jet lag.

entries.meaning: A member of the crew who looks after passengers on a plane. ---
examples: The flight attendant brought me a glass of water.
Two flight attendants worked the whole cabin.
Ask the flight attendant for a customs form.
entries.contrast: Modern American term; stewardess now sounds dated.

entries.meaning: The act of passing through a place on the way somewhere else, or public transportation as a system. ---
examples: We were in transit for almost thirty hours.
The city's public transit runs until midnight.
Passengers in transit stay in the secure area.

entries.meaning: The bags and suitcases a traveler takes on a trip. ---
examples: Baggage claim is downstairs to your left.
How much baggage are you checking?
All our baggage went to the wrong city.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: never baggages. Count with two pieces of baggage.

entries.meaning: An official document that proves your nationality and lets you travel abroad. ---
examples: My passport expires next spring.
Have your passports out for the officer.
He renewed his passport just in time.

entries.meaning: Official permission stamped in a passport to enter a country. ---
examples: You need a visa to work there.
Tourist visas are good for ninety days.
My visa application was approved.

entries.meaning: The government service that checks what travelers bring into a country. ---
examples: We got through customs in ten minutes.
Customs took away his oranges.
Fill out this form before you reach customs.
entries.contrast: Always ends in -s in this sense; a custom (singular) means a tradition.

entries.meaning: The desk or process where officials check travelers entering a country. ---
examples: The line at immigration was enormous.
Immigration asked how long I was staying.
You clear immigration before you pick up your bags.

entries.meaning: A place where officials stop people to inspect them or their documents. ---
examples: There's a security checkpoint before the gates.
We passed two checkpoints on the mountain road.
Take your laptop out at the checkpoint.

entries.meaning: An official statement listing what you are bringing into a country. ---
examples: Sign the customs declaration before landing.
The crew handed out declarations on the plane.
A false declaration can cost you a big fine.
entries.contrast: The verb declare stresses the second syllable: dih-KLAIR.

entries.meaning: The screening area and staff that check passengers before a flight. ---
examples: Get to the airport early; security is slow today.
Security made me throw out my water bottle.
We went through security in five minutes.

entries.meaning: An official paper allowing you to do something. ---
examples: You need a permit to camp in the canyon.
Permits sell out months in advance.
The ranger checked our permit at the trailhead.
entries.contrast: The noun is PUR-mit; the verb is pur-MIT.

entries.meaning: A document that shows who you are. ---
examples: You'll need photo identification to board.
The clerk asked for some form of identification.
Keep your identification somewhere safe.
entries.contrast: Shortened to ID in speech: Can I see your ID?

entries.meaning: The legal status of belonging to a particular country. ---
examples: She holds dual citizenship.
He applied for citizenship after five years.
Citizenship gives you the right to vote.

entries.meaning: The country a person legally belongs to. ---
examples: Write your nationality on line four.
Guests of twelve different nationalities stayed here.
The form asks for your nationality and date of birth.

entries.meaning: The office of a country's chief representative in a foreign capital. ---
examples: Call the embassy if you lose your passport.
Several embassies are on that street.
The embassy issued him emergency papers.

entries.meaning: A government office in a foreign city that helps its citizens and issues visas. ---
examples: I picked up my visa at the consulate.
There are consulates in three American cities.
The consulate is closed on national holidays.

entries.meaning: A period of being kept apart from others to stop disease from spreading. ---
examples: Arriving travelers were put in quarantine.
The dog spent two weeks in quarantine.
Quarantine rules changed while we were abroad.

entries.meaning: A paper or digital pass that lets you travel or enter a place. ---
examples: I bought a one-way ticket to Seattle.
The tickets were cheaper on a Tuesday.
Show your ticket to the conductor.

entries.meaning: An arrangement to hold a room, seat, or table for you. ---
examples: I made a reservation under Patterson.
All our reservations were canceled by the storm.
Do you have a reservation with us tonight?

entries.meaning: An arrangement made in advance to buy travel or a room. ---
examples: My booking number is in the email.
Hotel bookings are up this summer.
I changed the booking to a later date.

entries.meaning: A message or number proving that a booking was accepted. ---
examples: Bring a printed confirmation to the desk.
I never got the confirmations for either room.
Your confirmation should arrive within the hour.

entries.meaning: A printed slip that can be exchanged for goods or a service. ---
examples: The airline gave us a meal voucher.
Our tour price includes hotel vouchers.
Hand this voucher to the driver.

entries.meaning: A written plan of where you will go and when during a trip. ---
examples: Email me your itinerary before you fly.
The agency sent two possible itineraries.
Our itinerary has us in Rome by Thursday.

entries.meaning: The place you are traveling to. ---
examples: Our final destination is a village near the coast.
Beach destinations fill up fast in July.
We reached our destination well after dark.

entries.meaning: The money you pay to ride a bus, train, taxi, or plane. ---
examples: The bus fare went up to three dollars.
Airline fares drop after the holidays.
He paid my fare with his transit card.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like fair (just, or a county fair).

entries.meaning: A journey to a place and usually back again. ---
examples: We took a trip to the coast last weekend.
I make two trips a year to see my parents.
How was your trip?

entries.meaning: An act of traveling from one place to another, especially a long one. ---
examples: It was a long journey by bus and boat.
Their journeys across the desert took weeks.
The journey home felt twice as long.

entries.meaning: An organized visit to a place, often with a guide. ---
examples: We took a walking tour of the old city.
Boat tours leave every hour from the pier.
The tour lasts about ninety minutes.

entries.meaning: The business of providing travel and vacations for visitors. ---
examples: The island lives on tourism.
Tourism dropped sharply that winter.
She works in tourism down in Key West.

entries.meaning: A person who is making a trip. ---
examples: The traveler next to me slept the whole flight.
Business travelers board first.
Every traveler has to fill out this card.
entries.contrast: Spelled with one l in American English, two in British (traveller).

entries.meaning: A short trip made for pleasure, usually returning the same day. ---
examples: The ship offers excursions at every port.
We signed up for a day excursion to the volcano.
The excursion costs sixty dollars per person.

entries.meaning: An organized journey made for a particular purpose, often to a remote place. ---
examples: He joined an expedition to the Arctic.
Two expeditions reached the summit that season.
The expedition took four months to plan.

entries.meaning: An exciting or risky experience. ---
examples: Driving that road was quite an adventure.
She writes about her adventures in South America.
The whole trip turned into an adventure.

entries.meaning: A short vacation, usually somewhere relaxing. ---
examples: We booked a weekend getaway in the mountains.
Romantic getaways are their whole business.
That cabin makes a perfect getaway.

entries.meaning: A vacation taken by a couple right after their wedding. ---
examples: They spent their honeymoon in Hawaii.
Beach honeymoons are still the most popular.
We're saving up for a honeymoon in Italy.

entries.meaning: A trip to see or photograph wild animals, especially in Africa. ---
examples: They went on safari in Kenya.
Guided safaris start before sunrise.
The safari lasted five days.

entries.meaning: A vacation spent traveling on a large ship that stops at several ports. ---
examples: My grandparents took a cruise to Alaska.
Caribbean cruises are cheapest in the fall.
The cruise leaves from Miami on Sunday.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like crews (groups of workers).

entries.meaning: A long trip by sea or through space. ---
examples: The voyage across the Atlantic took nine days.
Their early voyages were mapped by hand.
It was the ship's final voyage.

entries.meaning: The activity of visiting interesting places as a tourist. ---
examples: We did some sightseeing before the meeting.
There's no time for sightseeing on this trip.
Sightseeing buses stop right outside the hotel.
entries.contrast: The sight- part sounds like site and cite.

entries.meaning: A journey to a holy or deeply meaningful place. ---
examples: She made a pilgrimage to the shrine every spring.
Thousands of pilgrimages end at that cathedral.
For him the trip was a kind of pilgrimage.

entries.meaning: A long, difficult walk, usually over rough country. ---
examples: The trek to base camp takes eight days.
They've done treks in Nepal and Peru.
It was a real trek up to the parking lot.

entries.meaning: A long walk in the country or mountains. ---
examples: We went on a short hike before breakfast.
The park has hikes for every level.
That hike nearly killed my knees.

entries.meaning: The activity of walking long distances in the countryside. ---
examples: Hiking is the main reason people come here.
Bring hiking boots and plenty of water.
We did a lot of hiking that summer.

entries.meaning: A traveler who goes cheaply from place to place carrying a large pack. ---
examples: A young backpacker asked us for directions.
The hostel is full of backpackers in August.
As a backpacker she saw twelve countries in a year.

entries.meaning: A building where travelers pay to stay overnight. ---
examples: Our hotel was two blocks from the beach.
All the hotels downtown were booked.
The hotel holds your bags after checkout.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: hoh-TEL, not HOH-tel.

entries.meaning: A roadside hotel where you park right outside your room. ---
examples: We stopped at a cheap motel off the interstate.
Old motels line that stretch of highway.
The motel had a vacancy sign out front.

entries.meaning: Cheap lodging where travelers sleep in shared rooms. ---
examples: We stayed in a hostel for twenty dollars a night.
The hostels here are clean and friendly.
The hostel has a kitchen you can use.
entries.contrast: Close to hostile (unfriendly); the two are easy to mix up.

entries.meaning: A small country hotel, often an old one. ---
examples: We spent the night at a little inn by the river.
The town has two inns and no hotels.
The inn serves breakfast until ten.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like the preposition in.

entries.meaning: A hotel or place built for vacations, with pools, restaurants, and activities. ---
examples: They stayed at a beach resort in Mexico.
Ski resorts open in late November.
The resort has three pools and a golf course.

entries.meaning: A hotel or large cabin in the mountains, woods, or a park. ---
examples: We booked a room at the park lodge.
Fishing lodges fill up early in the season.
The lodge has a huge stone fireplace.

entries.meaning: A large comfortable house, often rented for a vacation. ---
examples: They rented a villa with a private pool.
The villas sit on a hillside above the bay.
Our villa came with a cook.

entries.meaning: A small private house that rents rooms to travelers. ---
examples: We found a family guesthouse near the market.
Small guesthouses cost half what the hotels do.
The guesthouse only has six rooms.
entries.contrast: The u after g is silent: GEST, not GYOOST.

entries.meaning: The desk or area in a hotel where guests check in. ---
examples: Leave your key at reception when you go out.
Call reception if you need more towels.
The reception is open around the clock.

entries.meaning: A hotel employee who arranges tickets, tables, and tours for guests. ---
examples: The concierge got us a table for eight.
Two concierges work the evening shift.
Ask the concierge about the museum hours.
entries.contrast: French borrowing: the final -ge is the zh sound in measure.

entries.meaning: A hotel worker who carries guests' bags to their rooms. ---
examples: The bellhop took our suitcases upstairs.
Two bellhops were waiting by the door.
I tipped the bellhop five dollars.

entries.meaning: A person paid to carry luggage at a station, airport, or hotel. ---
examples: A porter helped us with the trunks.
The porters line up outside the station.
We hired a porter to carry the gear up the trail.

entries.meaning: The hotel staff and service that clean the rooms. ---
examples: Housekeeping comes around eleven.
I called housekeeping for extra pillows.
Hang the sign if you don't want housekeeping.

entries.meaning: A small refrigerator of drinks and snacks in a hotel room. ---
examples: Don't touch the minibar; it costs a fortune.
Some rooms have minibars and some don't.
He charged two sodas from the minibar.

entries.meaning: The time or act of leaving a hotel and paying at the end of a stay. ---
examples: Checkout is at eleven in the morning.
Late checkouts cost an extra thirty dollars.
We left our bags at the desk after checkout.

entries.meaning: The act of registering on arrival at a hotel or airport. ---
examples: Check-in starts at three o'clock.
Online check-ins open a day before the flight.
The check-in line stretched out the door.

entries.meaning: A feature or service that makes a place more comfortable. ---
examples: A gym is a standard amenity in that chain.
The listing describes all the amenities.
Free parking is the one amenity I actually use.

entries.meaning: A spot where you set up a tent or park a camper. ---
examples: We reserved a campsite by the lake.
All the campsites were taken by noon.
Our campsite had a fire ring and a picnic table.

entries.meaning: The activity of staying outdoors in a tent or camper. ---
examples: We go camping every Labor Day weekend.
Camping is not allowed outside the marked areas.
She bought all new camping gear.

entries.meaning: A shelter of cloth stretched over poles, used for sleeping outdoors. ---
examples: It took us an hour to put up the tent.
Three tents were pitched along the creek.
Rain came through the roof of the tent.

entries.meaning: An outdoor fire built at a camp for warmth or cooking. ---
examples: We sat around the campfire until midnight.
Campfires are banned during the dry season.
He cooked the whole dinner over a campfire.

entries.meaning: A vehicle without an engine that is pulled behind a car or truck. ---
examples: They tow a small trailer behind the pickup.
Half the trailers in the park are permanent.
We slept in the trailer instead of a tent.

entries.meaning: A large vehicle you can drive and live in on a trip. ---
examples: They toured the whole country in a motorhome.
Motorhomes need a special place to park overnight.
The motorhome sleeps six people.
entries.contrast: Usually called an RV in everyday American speech.

entries.meaning: A line of connected railroad cars pulled along tracks. ---
examples: The train to Boston leaves at 7:15.
Trains run every twenty minutes on weekdays.
We took the night train to save on a hotel.

entries.meaning: A building where trains or buses stop for passengers. ---
examples: Meet me at the station at six.
The line has forty stations.
There's a coffee shop inside the station.

entries.meaning: The raised walkway beside the track where passengers wait. ---
examples: Our train leaves from platform nine.
Both platforms were packed with commuters.
Stand back from the edge of the platform.

entries.meaning: A system of tracks and trains, or the company that runs it. ---
examples: The railroad runs right through the middle of town.
Two railroads merged last year.
His grandfather worked for the railroad.

entries.meaning: An underground city train system. ---
examples: Take the subway; it's faster than a cab.

The subway runs all night here.
entries.contrast: In the US a subway is the underground train; in Britain it is a pedestrian tunnel.

entries.meaning: A large road vehicle that carries many passengers. ---
examples: The airport bus leaves every fifteen minutes.
Two buses went by before ours came.
We took a bus across the state.
entries.contrast: Standard American plural is buses with one s; busses is rare.

entries.meaning: A bus or van that goes back and forth over a short route. ---
examples: The hotel shuttle picks you up at door three.
Shuttles run every ten minutes to the parking lot.
We missed the last shuttle and had to walk.

entries.meaning: A car with a driver that you pay to take you somewhere. ---
examples: We caught a taxi outside the terminal.
Taxis line up along the curb.
The taxi dropped us at the wrong hotel.

entries.meaning: A taxi, in everyday American speech. ---
examples: Let's just take a cab.
No cabs were out in that snowstorm.
The cab ride cost more than the train ticket.

entries.meaning: A separate closed section inside a vehicle or a piece of furniture. ---
examples: Put your bag in the overhead compartment.
The sleeper car has six compartments.
The maps are in the glove compartment.

entries.meaning: A main public road between towns and cities. ---
examples: Get on the highway and go north.
The state built two new highways out west.
There's a diner right off the highway.

entries.meaning: A wide highway with no traffic lights and no toll. ---
examples: The freeway was backed up for miles.
Los Angeles is built around its freeways.

entries.meaning: The way you go from one place to another. ---
examples: The scenic route adds an hour.
Both routes end up at the same lake.
We planned our route the night before.
entries.contrast: Many Americans also say it like rout, rhyming with out.

entries.meaning: Money you pay to use a road, bridge, or tunnel. ---
examples: The toll on that bridge is nine dollars.
Tolls add up fast on the turnpike.
We paid the toll with a transponder.

entries.meaning: A longer way around when the direct road is closed. ---
examples: Construction forced a detour through the old town.
There were two detours on the way up.
The detour cost us forty minutes.

entries.meaning: Something you pay to use for a while, especially a car. ---
examples: We picked up the rental at the airport.
Vacation rentals get expensive in July.
Return the rental with a full tank.

entries.meaning: The paved path along the side of a street for people on foot. ---
examples: Tables were set out on the sidewalk.
The sidewalks were icy that morning.
Walk on the sidewalk, not in the road.
entries.contrast: American sidewalk; the British say pavement.

entries.meaning: The marked strip where people are supposed to cross the street. ---
examples: Wait for the light and use the crosswalk.
The city painted new crosswalks downtown.
A car stopped short of the crosswalk.
entries.contrast: American crosswalk; the British say zebra crossing.

entries.meaning: A person walking rather than driving. ---
examples: A pedestrian stepped out in front of the bus.
Pedestrians have the right of way here.
That street is closed to cars and open to pedestrian traffic.

entries.meaning: The place where two roads cross. ---
examples: Turn left at the next intersection.
Three intersections down, you'll see the museum.
The intersection has a four-way stop.

entries.meaning: A circular junction that traffic drives around. ---
examples: Take the second exit off the roundabout.
The town put in two roundabouts last year.
I went around the roundabout twice by mistake.
entries.contrast: Also called a traffic circle in much of the US.

entries.meaning: Space where vehicles may be left, or the act of leaving them there. ---
examples: The hotel charges forty dollars for parking.
There's free parking behind the building.
Street parking is impossible on game days.

entries.meaning: The large window at the front of a car. ---
examples: A rock cracked our windshield on the highway.
Both windshields were covered in frost.
Clean the windshield before we drive at night.
entries.contrast: American windshield; the British say windscreen.

entries.meaning: A person who travels a distance to work and back every day. ---
examples: The 7:40 is packed with commuters.
As a commuter he spends two hours a day on the train.
Commuter traffic clears up after nine.
entries.русский: человек, ежедневно ездящий на работу издалека

entries.meaning: Someone who travels by getting free rides from passing drivers. ---
examples: We picked up a hitchhiker outside Reno.
You hardly see hitchhikers on this road anymore.
The hitchhiker was headed for the coast.

entries.meaning: A boat that carries people and cars regularly across water. ---
examples: The ferry to the island runs twice a day.
Both ferries were canceled because of wind.
We ate breakfast on the ferry.

entries.meaning: A large vessel that travels on the ocean. ---
examples: The cruise ship holds three thousand passengers.
Cargo ships waited outside the harbor.
Our ship docks at seven in the morning.

entries.meaning: A small vessel for traveling on water. ---
examples: We rented a boat for the afternoon.
Fishing boats filled the little harbor.

entries.meaning: An expensive boat used for pleasure trips or racing. ---
examples: A white yacht was anchored in the bay.
The marina is full of yachts in the summer.
They chartered a yacht for a week.
entries.contrast: The ch is silent: YAHT, not YATCH.

entries.meaning: A town or harbor where ships load and unload. ---
examples: The ship reached port just before dawn.
The cruise stops at four ports.
It's the busiest port on the coast.

entries.meaning: A structure at the edge of water where boats tie up. ---
examples: We waited on the dock for the ferry.
The old docks have been turned into restaurants.
He tied the boat to the dock.

entries.meaning: A long platform built out over water for boats or for walking. ---
examples: We walked out to the end of the pier.
Two wooden piers stretch into the lake.
There's a carousel on the pier.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like peer (to look closely, or an equal).

entries.meaning: A small harbor where private boats are kept. ---
examples: His sailboat is docked at the marina.
Both marinas were damaged by the hurricane.
There's a seafood place next to the marina.

entries.meaning: A tower with a bright light that warns ships of the shore. ---
examples: You can climb the lighthouse for three dollars.
Old lighthouses dot the whole coastline.
The lighthouse still flashes every ten seconds.

entries.meaning: A person who works on a ship or sails a boat. ---
examples: The sailor showed us how to tie the knot.
Sailors filled every bar in the port.

entries.meaning: A trip across water, or a place where you cross something. ---
examples: The crossing took six hours in rough seas.
There are two border crossings nearby.
Slow down at the railroad crossing.

entries.meaning: A well-known building or feature that helps you recognize a place. ---
examples: The old clock tower is a city landmark.
We saw all the usual landmarks in one day.
The bridge is the most photographed landmark here.

entries.meaning: A structure built to remember a person or an event. ---
examples: A stone monument stands in the square.
The park is full of war monuments.
They laid flowers at the monument.

entries.meaning: A very large and important church. ---
examples: The cathedral took two hundred years to build.

entries.meaning: A large old building with thick walls, built for defense. ---
examples: The castle sits on a hill above the river.

entries.meaning: A grand house where a ruler lives or once lived. ---
examples: The palace gardens are open to the public.

entries.meaning: What is left standing of an old destroyed building. ---

entries.meaning: A holy place devoted to a saint, god, or memory. ---
examples: Pilgrims come to the shrine every August.
Small shrines stand along the mountain path.

entries.meaning: A building where Muslims gather to pray. ---
examples: The blue mosque is the city's main sight.

entries.meaning: A structure that shoots water into the air, usually for decoration. ---
examples: Meet me by the fountain in the square.

entries.meaning: An open public square in a town or city. ---
examples: The band played in the main plaza.
Cafes surround both plazas.
Kids were kicking a ball around the plaza.

entries.meaning: A structure built to carry a road or path over water or a gap. ---
examples: The bridge is closed for repairs.

entries.meaning: A place that people come to see or enjoy. ---
examples: The falls are the biggest attraction in the state.

entries.meaning: A high spot with a view, usually with a place to park. ---

entries.meaning: A person who shows visitors around a place and explains it. ---

entries.meaning: A book of information for travelers visiting a place. ---

entries.meaning: A thin printed booklet advertising a place or service. ---
examples: The hotel brochure made the pool look bigger.

entries.meaning: A stiff card with a picture on one side, mailed without an envelope. ---
examples: She sent me a postcard from Lisbon.
I bought six postcards at the museum shop.
The postcard arrived two weeks after she got home.

entries.meaning: A large container of water built for swimming. ---
examples: The kids were in the pool all afternoon.
The resort has three pools and a hot tub.
Our room looks right out over the pool.

entries.meaning: A place offering massages, baths, and beauty treatments. ---
examples: She booked a massage at the hotel spa.
Mountain towns here are full of spas.
The spa opens at eight in the morning.

entries.meaning: A very hot wooden room used for sweating and relaxing. ---
examples: There's a sauna next to the locker room.
The gym has separate saunas for men and women.
Ten minutes in the sauna was plenty for me.

entries.meaning: A person paid to watch swimmers and rescue anyone in trouble. ---
examples: The lifeguard blew her whistle at us.
There are no lifeguards on duty after six.
Swim near the lifeguard stand.

entries.meaning: A short tube that lets you breathe while your face is in the water. ---
examples: Rent a mask and a snorkel at the beach hut.
The snorkels come with the boat tour.
Water kept getting into my snorkel.

entries.meaning: A long narrow board you stand on to ride ocean waves. ---
examples: He strapped the surfboard to the roof of the car.
Surfboards rent for twenty dollars a day.
Her surfboard is shorter than mine.

entries.meaning: Darker skin from spending time in the sun. ---
examples: She came back from Florida with a deep suntan.
Their suntans faded by October.
He got a suntan just sitting on the boat.

entries.meaning: A small stand or self-service machine where things are sold or printed. ---
examples: Print your ticket at the kiosk by the door.
All four kiosks were out of order.
We bought water from a kiosk on the corner.

entries.meaning: A thief who steals from people's pockets and bags in crowds. ---
examples: A pickpocket took his wallet on the subway.
Watch out for pickpockets around the station.
The pickpocket was gone before anyone noticed.

entries.meaning: A raised wooden path built along a beach for people to walk on.
examples: We walked the whole boardwalk after dinner.
Old boardwalks run along both beaches.
There's an ice cream stand at the end of the boardwalk.
